title: Business continuity assurance: inference SKU narrative for procurement and security
content:
Executive summary:

This note is a short narrative and procurement-ready checklist that frames Redwood’s dedicated inference offering as a business-continuity and risk-transfer product for platform, security, and finance stakeholders. The goal is to provide a concise, procurement-friendly storyline that complements technical throughput/SLA docs: explain what we guarantee, why that reduces operational risk, how fallback and escalation work, and what commercial constructs (commits, credits, carve-outs) map to buyer needs.

Audience:
- Primary: platform architects, SRE leads, procurement (platform spend), security/compliance reviewers.
- Secondary: finance and legal (TCO and penalty framing), product leaders evaluating uptime risk for user-facing features.

Core positioning (single-paragraph elevator):
Redwood Dedicated is sold as a business-continuity contract: customers buy predictable inference capacity with measurable SLOs, network and tenant isolation, and documented fallbacks so customer teams can design SLAs on top of our service without absorbing availability or queuing risk. That predictability converts to fewer incident-driven engineering hours, reduced failover complexity, and a clearer unit-cost model for product owners.

Key messages by stakeholder:
- Platform/SRE: predictable p99 latency and guaranteed concurrency means you can provision deterministic request pipelines and autoscale less aggressively; built-in region fallback and model-variant routing limits blast radius for incidents.
- Security/Compliance: Dedicated capacity isolates workloads (no multi-tenant runtime mixing), supports customer-managed KMS, and provides audit logs and private control plane options for regulated data.
- Finance/Procurement: Committed capacity reduces unit-cost variance and converts variable cloud spend into a predictable contract; SLA credits and a defined remediation ladder transfer measurable risk from the buyer to Redwood.

Measurable guarantees (framing for procurement brief):
- Throughput: committed throughput expressed as tokens/sec or concurrent requests for a named model family. Example: 1000 concurrent GPT-like requests (512-token avg) with sustained 99th-percentile response latency <= 300ms for the committed pool.
- Availability: control-plane availability SLA (e.g., 99.95%) plus serving-plane availability for committed capacity (e.g., 99.9%).
- Latency SLO: P95/P99 targets per class of request (interactive low-latency vs batch scoring).
- Incident MTTR commitments: targeted mean time-to-fallback (to warm region/variant) and mean time-to-recover for committed pool.
- Credits: a clear, limited credit schedule (e.g., percentage credit of monthly committed spend proportional to SLA breach severity).

Fallback and graceful degradation policy (operational narrative):
- Automatic local mitigation: queue shedding policy + prioritized token budget for high-priority routes.
- Cross-region fallback: transparent reroute to standby capacity (with documented latency and cost delta) when local pool degraded.
- Model-variant fallback: automatic switch to smaller/quantized model variant under sustained overload with explicit behavioral/quality notes and telemetry.
- Customer-visible state: incident page, per-tenant degraded-mode flag, and hooks for customer-side circuit breakers.

Procurement-ready commercial constructs (mapping options):
- Reserve + burst: base commit for predictable workload + measured burst reserve at a modeled premium (metered).
- Dedicated SKU tiers: Bronze/Silver/Gold mapped to throughput and MTTR targets (cheaper tiers have longer MTTR and less strict latency SLOs).
- Penalty ladder: credit scheme capped to a % of monthly committed spend; transparent formula tied to time and magnitude of SLA violation.
- Exit & transition: data transfer assistance and a runbook for customer self-hosted transition or burst to hosted variants for 90 days post-termination.

Procurement checklist (one-page for buyer packet):
- Define the committed capacity metric (concurrency, tokens/sec, or qps) and a representative request profile (avg tokens, prompt length distribution).
- Ask for historical production performance for the requested model family (p50/p95/p99, token throughput).
- Confirm isolation controls: dedicated pool topology, KMS integration, audit log retention and export.
- Validate fallback behaviors and expected customer impact (latency delta, quality regression notes).
- Confirm escalation path and named SLAs in contract (contacts, severity definitions, MTTR targets).
- Get clear credit schedule and calculation examples using the buyer’s expected usage pattern.
- Include a 30–90 day ramp plan and acceptance criteria for go-live (load tests, warm-up runbook).

Negotiation playbook (what to concede vs hold):
- Hold firm: core availability and latency SLOs for committed pool, and isolation guarantees. These are product differentiators and operationally expensive to promise if diluted.
- Flexible: ramp schedule, pricing for early-term burst capacity, and temporary pilot exceptions.
- Levers: shorten MTTR by investing in runbook integration during onboarding (chargeable), offer limited trial credits for high-severity buyers, or provide extended audit logs as an add-on.

Competitive differentiators to call out (concise):
- Unified rollout + observability: same controls and telemetry across hosted/dedicated/private reduces integration risk vs vendors who require distinct stacks.
- Programmable fallbacks: model-variant and region-level automatic routing that preserves throughput guarantees where possible.
- Cost-aware controls: per-route batching/caching knobs and recommended quantization profiles to trade quality vs unit-cost with measurable estimates.

Sample objection handling (short Q&A):
Q: Why can’t we just use large cloud VMs and manage inference ourselves?
A: Owning infra moves the SRE burden in-house; our value is operational ML inference expertise (KV cache, attention optimizations, efficient batching) plus a commercial SLA that transfers outage risk and reduces time-to-reliability.

Q: We worry about model quality when fallback occurs.
A: We provide documented quality deltas per fallback variant and telemetry hooks so buyers can detect and rollback to strict-mode if the quality impact is unacceptable.

Draft escalation ladder (example):
- Sev 3: non-critical degradation — on-call within 4 hours, advisory within 12 hours.
- Sev 2: partial capacity loss — on-call within 1 hour, mitigation plan within 4 hours, automated fallback engaged.
- Sev 1: committed pool outage — immediate page, local mitigation and cross-region fallback within 15 minutes, executive notification within 1 hour, recovery playbook initiated.

Contract language snippets (copy-paste friendly):
- "Committed Capacity": "Redwood will provision and reserve a dedicated inference pool sufficient to support the Committed Throughput (as defined in Schedule A) for the duration of the Term."
- "Availability": "Redwood will maintain Serving Availability for Committed Capacity at not less than 99.9% on a monthly basis. Availability shall be measured in accordance with the methodology defined in Schedule B."
- "Credits": "If Redwood fails to meet the Availability commitment for Committed Capacity, Customer shall be eligible for Service Credits per the Credit Schedule in Schedule C, subject to the conditions and limits therein."

Operational onboarding checklist (technical runbook summary):
- Provide representative traffic shape and sample prompts; run a 48–72h soak test during onboarding.
- Validate KMS integration and audit log streaming.
- Configure route priorities and local circuit-breakers; exercise fallback in a controlled window.
- Establish SLIs and dashboards in Redwood Console and agree on alert thresholds.

Metrics to include in Buyer Packet (data-backed persuasion):
- 30/60/90-day average p99 latency under committed load, with variance bands.
- Measured throughput per-model variant and expected token/sec after quantization profiles.
- Incident frequency and median MTTR for committed customers over the last 12 months.

Call script snippet for initial procurement meeting (30s opener):
"We position Redwood Dedicated not just as capacity but as a contract for predictability: it reduces your incident surface by guaranteeing throughput, isolation, and documented fallbacks that let your engineering teams design SLAs on top of our service without absorbing queuing or routing risk. Today I want to align on the workload profile so we can map you to the right committed SKU and provide concrete credit examples"

Next steps / immediate TODOs for the go-to-market team:
- Turn the procurement checklist into a one-page buyer packet and a 2-page tech appendix.
- Add a conservative credit-calculation spreadsheet (example scenarios: steady-state, 2x traffic surge, regional outage).
- Align with solutions engineering to produce three customer-ready acceptance test templates.

Notes to self (open questions to resolve before final):
- Formalize MTTR numbers based on ops telemetry and SRE capacity (proposal: 15min cross-region failover, 4h resolution for partial degradations).
- Create standardized language for quality deltas per model fallback variant.
- Decide default credit cap as a percent of committed monthly spend (benchmark options: 10% or 25%).

End of draft.

Recent edits: added procurement checklist and concrete commercial constructs (Aisha, 2025-02-18); refined fallback policy and escalation ladder (Marco, 2025-02-24); added sample contract snippets and call script (Evan, 2025-03-04).
